title: Mood Indigo, Solitude and Duke's own numbers
summary: Mood Indigo was part Duke and part Bigard; Dance discusses Solitude and numbers like Prelude to a Kiss that are all Duke.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Incidentally, we didn't talk about "Mood Indigo". Whose phrase was that, anyway? Can you think?
It was part him and part Barney Bigard.

And then I remember him saying that -- I remember the session in Chicago -- that was about '36, I think -- I remember he was saying -- he was leaning up, waiting to get into the record studio, and he was leaning up against the wall, and he had an envelope, and so he wrote "Solitude", wrote down the lead on "Solitude". I think that was all his.
Yeah. Well, I tell you what other numbers that seemed to be all his. You know how you can recognize a number as being a person's, you know, like, well, like Irving Berlin, or anybody.
Or, say, Cole Porter's. Well, to me the numbers that were very much his were -- wait a minute.
The two numbers I'm thinking about, Cootie, are "I've Got it Bad and That Ain't Good", and "Prelude to a Kiss". Those are totally Duke, wouldn't you say?
Well, I wouldn't know. To tell you the truth.
Why? Were you not there when they were written?
Well, you know, they have that -- they have a flavor to them, an odd flavor to them.
That I don't think anybody else -- you know, you can recognize. He did a few things like that. They weren't always very, very big. But they had that particular --

-- first of all, probably the chord progressions are unusual. And maybe even he wrote them in odd keys, too, they've got a funny sound to them. Are they, those keys, are they different? Can you think of them?
But all of his things that he did was pretty good. I thought. All of his numbers were good.
Yeah. They all had melody in them.
